title: Right hepatectomy
subtitle: Principles of liver resection: inflow, outflow, transection, Pringle

sources.title: The Brisbane 2000 terminology of liver anatomy and resections (Strasberg SM et al.)
Guidelines for perioperative care for liver surgery: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) Society recommendations (Melloul E et al., World J Surg)

sources.org: International Study Group of Liver Surgery (ISGLS)
sources.title: Posthepatectomy liver failure: a definition and grading by the International Study Group of Liver Surgery (Rahbari NN et al., Surgery)

sources.org: International Study Group of Liver Surgery (ISGLS)
sources.title: Bile leakage after hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery: a definition and grading of severity by the International Study Group of Liver Surgery (Koch M et al., Surgery)

indications: Colorectal liver metastases confined to the right hemiliver (or needing it), as part of an MDT plan with chemotherapy.
Hepatocellular carcinoma in a liver with adequate function and remnant, per a liver cancer MDT.
Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, selected hilar cholangiocarcinoma (usually extended, with caudate and bile duct resection), and gallbladder cancer requiring major resection.
Large symptomatic benign lesions, hydatid disease, living donor hepatectomy (specialist programmes), and some complex trauma.
This is a specialist operation; this outline teaches the principles of any anatomical liver resection.
contraindications: Insufficient future liver remnant volume or function for the quality of the liver; correct with portal vein embolisation or staged approaches, or do not resect.
Clinically significant portal hypertension or decompensated cirrhosis.
Disease in the remnant that cannot be cleared, or uncontrolled extrahepatic disease (per tumour type and MDT).
Physiological unfitness for a major operation with potential for large blood loss.
preparation: Cross-sectional imaging (contrast CT and liver MRI), staging per tumour type, MDT decision.

Assess the future liver remnant: CT volumetry, with liver quality (steatosis, chemotherapy injury, cirrhosis). Commonly cited minimum remnant volumes are about 20% in a normal liver, about 30% after extensive chemotherapy and about 40% in cirrhosis; follow the unit's protocol and consider portal vein embolisation.
Liver function: bilirubin, albumin, INR, platelets; Child-Pugh and MELD in cirrhosis; dynamic function tests where available.
Plan low central venous pressure anaesthesia with the anaesthetist; cross-match, cell saver.
Nutrition and prehabilitation; stop chemotherapy for the interval agreed with oncology.

Consent: bleeding and transfusion, bile leak, post-hepatectomy liver failure, ascites, collections, pleural effusion, air embolism, VTE, conversion of the planned resection, re-operation and mortality.
positioning: Supine, arms out, slight reverse Trendelenburg, with a bolster under the right side if helpful.
Arterial and central venous lines, urinary catheter, warming, calf compression; epidural or alternative analgesia per anaesthetic plan.
Low central venous pressure during transection achieved by the anaesthetist (fluid restriction and positioning); slight head-down tilt during transection reduces the risk of air embolism.
equipment: Major laparotomy set with a fixed costal-margin retractor.
Intra-operative ultrasound with a liver probe.
Transection device per unit practice: ultrasonic aspirator, clamp-crush with ties and clips, energy devices, water-jet; bipolar or saline-linked coagulation for the raw surface.
Vascular staplers for the portal pedicle and hepatic vein; vascular clamps and slings, including for the Pringle manoeuvre and the inferior vena cava.
anatomy: Couinaud's functional anatomy: the right hemiliver is segments 5 to 8, separated from the left by the plane of the middle hepatic vein (Cantlie's line, from the gallbladder fossa to the inferior vena cava).

Inflow: the right portal vein and right hepatic artery branch in the hilum; the right hepatic duct is short and its confluence with the left is variable, so it is best divided inside the liver or at the hilar plate.
Outflow: the right hepatic vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava, often with short accessory hepatic veins (including an inferior right hepatic vein) draining segments 6 and 7.
The middle hepatic vein drains segment 4 and parts of 5 and 8; preserving it with the left liver protects the remnant's outflow.
The caudate lobe (segment 1) drains directly into the inferior vena cava and is supplied from both sides.
criticalSafety: Confirm the plan on intra-operative ultrasound before any division.
Before ligating the right inflow, confirm the left portal vein and left hepatic artery supply the remnant (test clamp).
Divide the right hepatic duct away from the confluence to protect the left duct.
Transect along the demarcation line, staying to the right of the middle hepatic vein.
Keep the central venous pressure low during transection, and record all Pringle times.
structuresAtRisk: Left portal vein, left hepatic artery and left hepatic duct (the remnant's inflow and drainage)
Inferior vena cava and right adrenal vein
commonErrors: Ligating the right portal pedicle en bloc too close to the confluence, injuring the left duct or left portal vein.
Avulsing short hepatic veins by rotating the liver forcefully off the inferior vena cava.
Transecting under a high central venous pressure, with constant hepatic venous back-bleeding.
Drifting into the middle hepatic vein or the left liver during transection.
Not recognising post-hepatectomy liver failure early.
complications: Bile leak and biloma, graded by ISGLS.
Post-hepatectomy liver failure (ISGLS: raised INR and hyperbilirubinaemia on or after day five).
Ascites, pleural effusion, subphrenic collection, air embolism.
postop: Level 2 or 3 care initially; ERAS for liver surgery where appropriate.
Daily bilirubin, INR, lactate, renal function and glucose; watch for liver failure (rising bilirubin and INR after day five, encephalopathy, ascites).
Phosphate replacement: hypophosphataemia is common during regeneration.
Drain (if placed) for bile; investigate bilious output with imaging and consider ERCP or percutaneous drainage.
Pharmacological thromboprophylaxis once haemostasis allows; MDT review of histology and margins.

steps.emphasis: Remnant volume and liver quality documented, portal vein embolisation result if done, chemotherapy interval, and the planned resection named in Brisbane 2000 terms.
Agree low central venous pressure targets, blood availability, cell saver and Pringle timing with the anaesthetist.
Supine, slight reverse Trendelenburg for mobilisation; the anaesthetist may tilt head-down during transection to reduce air embolism risk.
Prepare the chest as well, in case a thoracoabdominal extension or pleural drain is needed.
Reversed L (J) or rooftop incision; divide the falciform ligament up to the suprahepatic inferior vena cava to expose the hepatic vein confluence.
Map every lesion, the middle and right hepatic veins and the left pedicle; mark the middle hepatic vein on the surface. Confirm nothing in the remnant changes the plan.

Cholecystectomy, then hilar dissection: identify the right hepatic artery and right portal vein, and confirm the left hepatic artery and left portal vein before anything is divided. Sling the hepatoduodenal ligament for a Pringle.
Intermittent clamping during transection, commonly in cycles of about 15 minutes with about 5 minutes of reperfusion, per unit protocol; record the total time.

Liver bleeding: inflow is controlled by the Pringle; back-bleeding needs a lower central venous pressure, compression and suture of the hepatic vein branch. Caval injury: compress, control, repair with fine monofilament; pack if physiology fails.
White test or leak test through the cystic duct stump; suture leaking ducts on the cut surface.
With the Pringle off and the central venous pressure restored towards normal, inspect the cut surface, the diaphragm, the adrenal and the caval bed.
Selective, per unit policy; if placed, it is for early warning of bile leak or bleeding.
Mark the transection margin and any close margin; ink per pathology protocol.
Before closing, fix the falciform ligament back to stop the remnant rotating and kinking the left hepatic vein outflow.
Record resection in Brisbane terms, total Pringle time, blood loss, remnant appearance and colour, bile leak test, and the liver failure watch plan.

step.hep.mobilise.title: Mobilising the right liver off the diaphragm and the vena cava
step.hep.mobilise.why: The right liver is held by its triangular and coronary ligaments and drained by short veins into the inferior vena cava. Mobilisation brings the right hepatic vein and the vena cava into view and allows the liver to be compressed and controlled if it bleeds.
how: Divide the right triangular and coronary ligaments and separate the bare area from the diaphragm, rotating the liver gently to the left.
Separate the right adrenal gland from the liver, ligating the adrenal vein if necessary.
Working from below, ligate and divide the short hepatic veins on the anterior surface of the inferior vena cava, one by one, including any inferior right hepatic vein.
Divide the inferior vena cava (hepatocaval) ligament, which may contain a vein, to expose the right hepatic vein's posterior aspect.
structuresAtRisk: Inferior vena cava and short hepatic veins
pitfalls: Forceful rotation that avulses a short hepatic vein from the cava.
Tearing the diaphragm, causing a pneumothorax; repair it and tell the anaesthetist.
Approaching a very large tumour by mobilisation first; consider an anterior approach (transection before mobilisation) instead.

step.hep.inflow.title: Inflow control: right hepatic artery and right portal vein
step.hep.inflow.why: Dividing the right-sided inflow before transection reduces bleeding and produces a visible demarcation line that marks the true plane between the right and left liver. Dividing the wrong vessel devascularises the remnant.
how: Test-clamp the right hepatic artery and confirm a pulse in the left hepatic artery; then ligate and divide it.

Isolate the right portal vein, ligating the small caudate branch from its back if it is in the way, test-clamp and confirm left portal flow (ultrasound helps); then divide it with a vascular stapler or oversewn ties.
Leave the right hepatic duct to be divided during transection or at the hilar plate, away from the confluence.
Watch the demarcation line appear on the liver surface and compare it with the ultrasound mark of the middle hepatic vein.
Alternative: extrahepatic Glissonean pedicle control (taking the right pedicle en bloc above the hilar plate), in experienced hands.
structuresAtRisk: Left hepatic duct and the biliary confluence
pitfalls: Ligating the right portal vein too close to the bifurcation, narrowing the left portal vein.
Dividing the right hepatic duct close to the confluence, injuring the left duct.
Assuming the artery on the right is the right hepatic artery without tracing it.

step.hep.outflow.title: Outflow control: the right hepatic vein
step.hep.outflow.why: Controlling the right hepatic vein reduces back-bleeding during transection and avoids a catastrophic tear at the end of the operation. It is a short, wide vein entering the cava directly, so a slip here bleeds fast and allows air embolism.
how: With the liver mobilised and the caval ligament divided, develop the space between the right and middle hepatic veins from above and pass a clamp or sling around the right hepatic vein.
Divide it with a vascular stapler, or between vascular clamps with an oversewn caval stump, with the anaesthetist warned.
If extrahepatic control is not safe (large tumour near the vein), control and divide the vein inside the liver at the end of transection instead.
Ensure the middle hepatic vein is preserved for the remnant.
pitfalls: Blunt dissection around the vein behind a large tumour, tearing it.
A stapler that catches the middle hepatic vein or narrows the cava.

step.hep.transection.title: Parenchymal transection along the demarcation line
step.hep.transection.why: Transection is where most blood is lost and where the remnant's outflow and bile ducts can be injured. A low central venous pressure, an intermittent Pringle and a consistent technique keep the plane dry and visible, and keep the remnant intact.
how: Ask the anaesthetist to keep the central venous pressure low (commonly quoted as below about 5 cm H2O) before starting.
Score the liver capsule along the demarcation line, checked against the ultrasound mark; place stay sutures on either side.
Fracture the parenchyma with the chosen device (ultrasonic aspirator, clamp-crush), exposing vessels and ducts; ligate or clip anything larger than a couple of millimetres, and seal smaller ones.
Stay to the right of the middle hepatic vein, ligating segment 5 and 8 branches entering it; re-check the plane with ultrasound if unsure.
Divide the right hepatic duct inside the liver at the level of the hilar plate, and the right hepatic vein if not controlled earlier, with a stapler.
structuresAtRisk: Inferior vena cava at the end of transection
pitfalls: Transecting while the central venous pressure is high, causing constant back-bleeding.
Curving the plane into the left liver or into the middle hepatic vein.
Tearing a hepatic vein branch by pulling the specimen apart too forcefully.
